text.text: The first two weeks decide whether a project runs on time. This is the kickoff we run for every new app, from signed contract to the first sprint.
Project created under the client with a lead and a target launch date
Client named one product owner who can say yes and no
Developer accounts: the client owns their Apple Developer and Google Play accounts and adds us as team members
Access to any system the app talks to: payments, bookings, a test account
The client tells us who uses the app and the one job it must do well.
We walk through the signed scope screen by screen. Anything not on the list is written down as a possible
, a demo at the end of each, and who from the client attends.
Agree how bugs are reported and how fast we answer.
Set the milestones: design sign-off, prototype, feature complete, QA pass, store submission, client training.
Interview five real users if the client can arrange it.
Map every screen and the path between them.
List the risky parts: a payment provider, an old booking system, offline use.
End with a demo of the screen map and a revised estimate. If the estimate grows, say so now.
Design runs one sprint ahead of build. The client signs off each screen group before it is built; changes after sign-off are change requests.

Sunrise Language Academy signed a time-and-materials contract for a lesson booking app. In discovery, interviews showed teachers mostly use phones between classes, so the plan put the teacher schedule first. A waitlist for full lessons came up and was logged as a change request rather than squeezed in.
Shipping to the App Store and Google Play is its own small project. Apple's review usually takes a day or two and can reject a build for reasons that have nothing to do with code. Plan for it.
Store listing written: name, subtitle, description, keywords, support link, privacy policy link
Screenshots for every required phone and tablet size
Privacy answers for both stores match what the app really collects
Test accounts for reviewers, with a note on how to reach every feature
No open critical bugs on the project (
The client has tested the release build on their own phones and said yes in writing.
Crash reporting and analytics are switched on for the release build.
Sign-in works for a new user, a returning user and someone who deleted the app.
. Watch the review status daily. Release manually rather than automatically, so the client can announce it.
and copy the reviewer's words into

. Most rejections are about sign-in options, payments for digital goods, missing privacy details or a demo account that does not work. Fix, reply in the review thread, and resubmit the same day if you can.
Release in the store, check the listing live, install from the store on a clean phone.
Watch crash reports for 48 hours. A crash rate above one percent of sessions means a fix release.
Tell the client what to expect in reviews and how to answer them.
Phased release on the App Store lets you pause if something breaks. Google Play staged rollouts work the same way; start at 20 percent.

Loyalty cards 1.1 was rejected because it offered social sign-in without Sign in with Apple. The team added it in a day, resubmitted with a note to the reviewer, and the build was approved the next afternoon. The rejection reason went into the kickoff checklist for the next project.
Every agency loses money in the gap between what was signed and what the client remembers asking for. Change requests close that gap politely and in writing.

Anything not in the signed scope: a new screen, a new integration, a second language, a different way of doing something already signed off. Bug fixes are not changes. Polish inside an agreed screen usually is not either; use judgment and be generous with small things.

The change still gets logged and estimated, so the client sees what they are buying and the launch date stays honest.

Greenfield Clinic Group asked for a Spanish version two weeks before launch. The lead estimated nine days, priced it at the project's day rate and showed it would move launch by two weeks. The clinic chose to launch in English on time and approve Spanish for the first update.
